title: Battles in the Supreme Court -- Ch. 1: A WINDOW TO THE COURT
keywords: no power blocs, cliques, coteries, factions or groupings
the three rounds in the Supreme Court
St. Martin's Funeral Homes v. NLRC
primary_topics: Chapter 1 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' -- CJP's opening of 'a little window' on how the Supreme Court actually works, written to mark his third anniversary on the Court (October 10, 1998) and to show the judicial independence Chief Justice Narvasa said he was proudest of

His categorical testimony from inside: in three years he perceived no improper political, ideological or partisan alignment, no power blocs or factions, no justice asking him to vote a particular way -- not even the Chief Justice, the Court's primus inter pares

A procedural anatomy of the Court: a review court that acts only when asked; collegial decision-making in which no justice can individually bind the Court; agendas of 150 to 250 items; seating by seniority; the three divisions; robes, sessions and forms of address

The 'three rounds' a case must survive -- the procedural and substantive screening of the First Round with its twenty-one grounds for dismissal by minute resolution, the comment-and-reply exchange of the Second, and the memoranda, deliberation, ponencia and nominal voting of the Third

Delay and the backlog: the Court disposes of roughly as many cases as are filed (13,784 decided against 13,740 filed on average), but carries an inherited backlog he estimated at about 2,000, which the transfer of NLRC review to the Court of Appeals should help relieve
sub_topics: The opening scene: at Chief Justice Narvasa's March 26, 1998 farewell to the Manila Overseas Press Club, asked what he considered the most important feature of his term, Narvasa said he was proudest of the Court's independence in deciding cases, especially those affecting the President
The charge CJP answers: allegations that some justices, particularly appointees of President Fidel V. Ramos, had shown undue bias in lining up votes to uphold the President's decisions

His testimony: since October 10, 1995 no justice has faced serious indictment for voting out of gratitude to the appointing power; there are no power blocs or coteries as those terms are used in Congress; he has never been asked or influenced to vote in any particular manner, and has tangled with every member including the Chief Justice, with disagreements confined to the four walls of the session halls

The book's purpose and limit: to commemorate his third anniversary by writing his impressions of the judicial battles he took part in -- not briefs or oral jousts, but the closed-door deliberations attended by justices alone -- without violating the confidential and delicate nature of those processes

The Court as a review court: it affirms, modifies or reverses decisions of lower courts or determines whether a court, branch or instrumentality acted without or in excess of jurisdiction or with grave abuse of discretion; it does not initiate review, so the judiciary is 'a passive branch,' with automatic review of death sentences the possible exception

Transparency below, confidentiality above: Justice Florenz D. Regalado's formulation that in trial courts the rule is transparency but in the Supreme Court it is confidentiality, only the net results being released to the public

Collegiality in practice: all actions are determined in session, even motions for extension; agendas run 150 to 250 items; the backbreaking work is done in chambers and at home; verbal discussion is limited and, when it exceeds five minutes, the Chief Justice postpones it so members can write opinions pro and contra

Oral arguments: rare, held in the cavernous hearing hall on Padre Faura for difficult cases, twenty minutes a side but usually extended by questions, sometimes with amici curiae -- a rare privilege granted to lawyers of unquestioned stature, and once to Archbishop Oscar V. Cruz at CJP's instance

Sessions and protocol: en banc every Tuesday and in division Mondays and Wednesdays at 10:00 a.m.; strict seniority in seating, which he reproduces as of October 10, 1998 with each justice's retirement date; business suits or barong for internal sessions, all-black working robes for oral arguments and purple-bordered ceremonial robes for official functions; the title 'Justice' reserved by Court resolution to members of the Supreme Court, Court of Appeals and Sandiganbayan

The First Round: the Court may dismiss motu proprio, and he lists twenty-one procedural and substantive grounds -- late filing, defective service or verification, unpaid docket fees, missing material dates, no certification of no forum shopping, failure to show reversible error or grave abuse, wrong mode of appeal, violation of the hierarchy of courts, certiorari as a substitute for a lost appeal -- disposed of by minute resolutions in standard forms

The Second Round: comments, reply, rejoinder and even sur-rejoinder, ending either in due course or in an extended resolution -- and his correction of the lawyers' belief that such unsigned resolutions are written by the clerk of court, who is barred from deliberations

The Third Round: memoranda, deliberation, assignment of a ponente, promulgation, and a fifteen-day non-extendible period for reconsideration; about ninety percent of decisions are unanimous, and when the Court divides it votes nominally from the most junior upward so new justices are freed of the influence of their seniors

Delay and the numbers: drawing on three Annual Reports, he shows output roughly matching input, identifies a backlog of cases submitted more than twenty-four months earlier, and welcomes St. Martin's Funeral Homes v. NLRC, which sent NLRC judgments to the Court of Appeals first and should cut new filings by about twenty percent

Why the Court of Appeals route will not prolong cases: 51 justices in 17 divisions act faster, not all CA decisions are appealed, and by his own estimate only about twenty percent of CA petitions reach a penned decision, of which half are affirmed -- a ten percent chance of reversal

The comparison with the United States Federal Supreme Court, which issues about 200 penned decisions a year and has no backlog because its jurisdiction is narrower and it is extra selective in granting due course

The Court's other burdens: administrative supervision of the judiciary and the legal profession, the IBP's slow investigation of lawyers under the self-policing policy, and criminal appeals imposing death or reclusion perpetua that cannot be refused and account for half of all penned decisions

How cases are assigned: docketing, a three-justice raffle committee that decides banc or division, a confidential raffle in which the ponente surfaces only at the session and is named publicly only upon promulgation, and the per curiam tradition in death and dismissal cases -- a practice about which he records personal reservations

What the ponente does in each round, from recommending outright denial to preparing an abstract and a draft decision that the justices may affirm, amend, modify or refer to the banc, with votes finally manifested by signatures on the ponencia -- and the closing point that the real battles take place in the banc

stances.claim: The Supreme Court of his first three years was genuinely independent: there were no power blocs, cliques or factions, no justice ever asked him to vote in a particular way, and no group of justices voted out of gratitude to the appointing power.
stances.rhetorical_move: first-hand categorical testimony from an insider, offered against named public allegations and qualified by footnoted exceptions rather than by denial

stances.claim: Opening a window on the Court's unwritten practices serves the public understanding of judicial decision-making without violating the confidentiality of deliberations, which remain the Court's rule as against the transparency of trial courts.
stances.rhetorical_move: sets the limits of his own disclosure before making it, distinguishing procedure and practice (which he will describe) from the content of deliberations (which he will not)

stances.claim: The Court's delay is a backlog problem rather than an output problem: it decides about as many cases as are filed each year, and the inherited backlog of roughly 2,000 submitted cases can only be cut by reducing new filings -- which the transfer of NLRC review to the Court of Appeals should do by about twenty percent.
stances.rhetorical_move: answers a common public lament with three years of Annual Report statistics and his own estimates, then offers an institutional remedy

stances.claim: The per curiam practice of withholding the names of authors in death-penalty and dismissal decisions should be reconsidered, since lower court magistrates are named and Supreme Court justices should not be excepted.
stances.rhetorical_move: registers a personal reservation in a footnote, framed as a question rather than a demand

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' opened what CJP called a little window on how the Court works, written to mark his third anniversary as a justice on October 10, 1998. He began with Chief Justice Andres R. Narvasa's March 1998 farewell to the Manila Overseas Press Club, where Narvasa said he was proudest of the Court's independence in deciding cases affecting the President, and answered the charge that appointees of President Fidel V. Ramos had lined up their votes for him: in three years, CJP wrote, he had perceived no improper political, ideological or partisan alignment, no power blocs, cliques, coteries or factions, and no justice, not even the primus inter pares, had asked him to vote a particular way. Promising not to violate the confidentiality of deliberations, he described instead the Court's unwritten practices. The Court is basically a review court, passive until a petition is filed, deciding whether a lower court or any branch of government committed reversible error or grave abuse of discretion. Its work is collegial: no justice can bind the Court alone, agendas run to 150 to 250 items, discussion is brief and argument is written rather than spoken, and oral arguments with amici curiae are rare. He set out the seniority protocol, the divisions, robes and sessions, then traced the three rounds a case passes through, listing twenty-one grounds for dismissal by minute resolution in the first, the comment-and-reply exchange in the second, and memoranda, deliberation, a ponencia and nominal voting from the most junior justice upward in the third. Turning to delay, he used three years of Annual Reports to show output matching input and blamed an inherited backlog of about 2,000 cases, welcoming the transfer of NLRC review to the Court of Appeals. He closed with how cases are raffled and assigned, his reservation about per curiam anonymity, and the observation that the real battles occur in the banc.
